subject: Accounting
title: Activity-Based Costing
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Activity-Based Costing.

hook.text: Two products use the same machine hours but different amounts of setup time. Traditional costing treats them the same.

buildup.text: Activity-based costing assigns overhead based on the actual activities that drive costs.

discovery.text: It identifies cost drivers—setups, inspections, orders—and traces costs to products that consume them.

twist.text: ABC often reveals that high-volume products subsidize low-volume ones—a hidden cross-subsidy.

climax.text: More accurate product costs lead to better pricing, better mix decisions, and higher profits.

punchline.text: Costs should follow the activities that cause them.

quiz.question: What does activity-based costing use to assign overhead?
options: The actual activities that drive costs

details.summary: Activity-based costing assigns overhead costs to products based on the activities that drive those costs, rather than spreading them evenly. This topic explains how ABC identifies cost drivers, traces resources to activities, and produces more accurate product costs.
details.whyItMatters: Traditional overhead allocation can make low-volume products look cheap and high-volume products look expensive. ABC reveals true costs so managers make better pricing and product-mix decisions.
takeaways: ABC traces overhead to activities like machine setups, inspections, or order processing
Cost drivers are the measurable factors that cause an activity's cost to increase
ABC is most valuable when products vary significantly in complexity and volume

faq.question: What is activity-based costing?
faq.answer: Activity-based costing is a method that assigns overhead costs to products based on the activities they actually consume—like the number of machine setups, quality inspections, or purchase orders—rather than using a single allocation base like direct labor hours.

faq.question: When should a company use activity-based costing?
faq.answer: ABC is most beneficial when a company produces a diverse mix of products with different complexity levels, when overhead is a large percentage of total costs, or when traditional costing produces costs that seem out of line with market prices.
